The exponential is (1/2) exp(−5n/s). The auxiliary moment has the prescribed tilt (4ns+(s−1)^2)/(8n(n−1)), sign (−1)^n and real exponent (n : ℝ)/2; the numerator q^n uses the natural exponent n.
semantic_slots.conclusion: The owner and anonymous target give both non-strict comparisons (1/2) exp(−5n/s) ≤ q^n/(2+4ns/(s+1)^2) ≤ δ, as a conjunction with the identical intermediate ratio. This is precisely the candidate chain, not merely its transitive endpoint.
semantic_slots.senses: The two sign priors condition the same full Haar probability; measure bind integrates the Gaussian event masses. Normalized event TV is sup_B |P₊(B)−P₋(B)|, not the unhalved L¹ density distance; this real supremum is nonempty and bounded by one. No statement of attainment, sharpness or equality of TV with the test gap.

mathematics_checks: A fixed reflection preserves Haar under left multiplication and swaps the measurable determinant classes, which partition O(n), so each has mass 1/2. Since ⟨x,Ox⟩ ≤ ‖x‖² and κ−1 ≥ 0, xᵀA_Ox ≥ ‖x‖², making the symmetric inverse a genuine Gaussian covariance. With the established measurable kernel, both bind mixtures are probabilities.

For λ ≥ 0 the radial test is Borel and in [0,1], so the kernel integrals are bounded and the sign split gives 2H(λ) = E₊h−E₋h. Integrating 1_{u<h(x)} over [0,1] and using nonnegative Tonelli yields the stated layer-cake formula and comparison with δ without another factor of two. The Lean Eq20 route identifies the Gaussian density and instead uses a Bernoulli test kernel with TV contraction.

s ≥ 2 and n ≥ 3 give s+1 > 0, n > 0, n−1 > 0, 0 < a,q,r < 1, and λ_* > 0. Eq24 in EvaluatedGaussian evaluates the same Gaussian-kernel integral and its density representative. Hence 2|H(λ_*)| = 2q^n a^(n/2)/(n(1−r²)); the sign disappears in both parities. The real power on positive a is convex for n/2 ≥ 1 and its tangent at one gives a^(n/2) ≥ 1/2, including odd n.

The identities 1−q² = 4s/(s+1)^2 and n(1−a²) = 2−1/n give n(1−r²) = 4ns/(s+1)^2 + q²(2−1/n). The final summand is at most 2, so 0 < n(1−r²) ≤ D; replacing the positive denominator by the larger D lowers the positive ratio in the required direction.

Since s−1 ≥ s/2 > 0, log(1/q) = log(1+1/s)+log(1+1/(s−1)) ≤ 3/s via log(1+t) ≤ t. Thus q^n ≥ exp(−3n/s). From (s+1)^2 ≥ s² and 1+t ≤ exp(t), D ≤ 2(1+2n/s) ≤ 2 exp(2n/s). The numerator lower bound divided by the positive denominator upper bound is exactly (1/2) exp(−5n/s). NumericSeparation proves this same scalar comparison for the exact domain.
